title: Zhuge Liang's Empty Fort
text:
One of the most famous stories of the Three Kingdoms is a bluff. The oldest version survives because the historian Pei Songzhi, in the 5th century, quoted it in his commentary on Chen Shou's Records of the Three Kingdoms, attributing it to an earlier writer, Guo Chong.

In Guo Chong's account, Zhuge Liang, chancellor of Shu, was at Yangping with only a small force after sending most of his troops away. The Wei general Sima Yi approached with a large army. Zhuge Liang's officers were terrified. Instead of fleeing or barricading the walls, Zhuge Liang ordered the flags lowered and the drums silenced, and had the city gates thrown open with men sweeping the ground in front of them. Sima Yi, who knew Zhuge Liang as a careful commander who never took needless risks, suspected a hidden ambush and withdrew his army.

Pei Songzhi himself doubted the story. He pointed out that Sima Yi was serving far away at the time and that the details did not fit the known record. Centuries later the novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms moved the scene to a town called Xicheng and added the most famous image: Zhuge Liang sitting calmly on the wall, playing the zither, while the enemy army hesitated below.
lesson: A reputation for caution can make a bold move believable. Know what your opponent expects of you, because his expectations can be used as much as your resources.
location: Yangping (modern Shaanxi, China) in the earliest version
source: Guo Chong, quoted by Pei Songzhi in his commentary on Chen Shou, Records of the Three Kingdoms (Sanguozhi); Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms, chapter 95
caveat: Already in the 5th century Pei Songzhi judged the episode untrue, and the zither scene is fiction from the novel.
